group_assessment.weighting: A neuron-specific Depdc5 conditional knockout mouse (6-9 weeks), rat primary cortical neurons with shRNA knockdown, HEK293T and HeLa lines, and a PTZ seizure assay. Primary for the DEPDC5/GATOR1 mTORC1 axis, not for WWOX and not for any neonatal or encephalopathic-feeding question. The observation (24 h fasting lowers PTZ seizure incidence in control mice and not in Depdc5 knockout mice; fasting lowers cortical pS6) is firm as reported; the interpretation that nutrient sensing upstream of mTORC1 mediates fasting protection is the authors' inference from one knockout. Not a WWOX system.

entries.proposition: In wild-type mice, 24 h fasting reduced PTZ-induced generalised seizures from 56% to 22%.
entries.snippet: Fasting for 24 h significantly reduced PTZ-induced seizures from 56% having seizures in the fed state to 22% in fasted mice

entries.proposition: Figure 1B shows the wild-type fed and fasted cumulative seizure curves (fed plateau near 56%, fasted near 20%); the panel agrees with the text.
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure 1B: wild-type mice, PTZ-induced seizures (% of total) against time to 1200 s; the fed curve plateaus near 56% and the fasted curve near 20%, asterisk marking the difference.

experimental_context.system: wild-type mouse, 6-9 weeks, 24 h food withdrawal with water ad lib, PTZ 65 mg/kg i.p.
experimental_context.endpoint: generalised tonic-clonic seizure incidence over 20 min

entries.proposition: Fasting did not change seizure latency or duration in wild-type mice; the effect is on incidence only.
entries.snippet: There was no effect on seizure latency or seizure duration (Figures S1A and S1B).

entries.proposition: Fasting protection was lost in neuron-specific Depdc5 knockout mice.
entries.snippet: Fasting for 24 h failed to protect Depdc5cc + mice from PTZ-induced seizures, whereas littermate controls continued to demonstrate a protective effect from fasting (Figure 1E).

entries.proposition: Figure 1E: the cKO fed and fasted curves (about 79% and 75%) lie above both control curves and nearly overlap; the control fasted curve is lowest (about 31%).
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure 1E: four cumulative seizure curves; Depdc5 cKO fed (about 79%) and fasted (about 75%) nearly overlap above control fed (about 62%) and control fasted (about 31%).

experimental_context.system: neuron-specific Depdc5 conditional knockout versus littermate control, 24 h fast, PTZ 65 mg/kg

entries.proposition: Fasting lowered blood glucose and raised beta-hydroxybutyrate in the knockout as in controls, yet gave it no seizure protection.
entries.snippet: Depdc5 neuronal-specific knockout mice had reductions in blood glucose, several amino acids, and increases in ketones upon fasting, yet the mice were not protected from seizures.

entries.proposition: Fasting-induced ketosis was larger in the knockout than in controls.
entries.snippet: Fasting induced ketosis as measured by elevated 3-hydroxybutanonic acid (e.g., beta-hydroxybutyrate) in both genotypes with higher levels in Depdc5cc+ mice compared with controls (Figure S1I).

entries.proposition: The fasting protocol removed food for 24 h with water available, and tested at 6-9 weeks; no calorie, dextrose or fluid-volume arm exists.
entries.snippet: Mice were weighed followed by food removal at 1pm for 24hr with ad lib water access.

entries.proposition: Whole-cortex amino acid changes after fasting: glutamine and arginine lower, more so in the knockout; leucine rises less in the knockout.
entries.snippet: Not only was glutamine reduced in the fasted state, but glutamine was further reduced in the Depdc5cc+ brains compared with controls regardless of the fed or fasted state (Figure 4C).

entries.proposition: The only deaths after PTZ occurred in knockout mice and fasting did not prevent them (Figure 4H shows death only in the two knockout curves).
entries.snippet: Only Depdc5cc+ mice died from PTZ-induced seizures and fasting had no effect on seizure-induced death (Figure 4H).

entries.proposition: Figure 4H panel: control fed and fasted curves stay at zero deaths; cKO fed plateaus near 26% and cKO fasted near 40%.
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure 4H: seizure-induced death (% of total seizures) against latency to death; control fed and control fasted stay at 0%, Depdc5 cKO fed plateaus near 26% and cKO fasted near 40%.

experimental_context.system: neuron-specific Depdc5 conditional knockout versus littermate control

entries.proposition: Figure S1 (supplement) shows the fasted wild-type blood glucose near 100 mg/dL against about 190 fed and weight change near -15%; plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate about 1.4 mM control and about 2 mM knockout after fasting.
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure S1 (supplement page 2): panel C weight change about -15% fasted; panel D blood glucose about 190 fed and about 100 mg/dL fasted; panel I plasma 3-hydroxybutyric acid about 0.4 mM fed, about 1.4 (control) and about 2 mM (knockout) fasted.
entries.anchor: Supplementary Figure S1C, D, I (supplement PDF page 2)

entries.proposition: The authors conclude that DEPDC5-related epilepsy may be insensitive to nutrient manipulation and that the pathway may still serve other causes.
entries.snippet: While DEPDC5-related epilepsy may be insensitive to nutrient manipulation, the nutrient-sensing pathways through mTOR may be a potential therapeutic strategy for treating seizures of other causes.

entries.proposition: The authors state the gap between primary neuronal cultures and the mature brain and that shRNA leaves residual protein.
entries.snippet: While our in vitro data are compelling, there are still large gaps between primary neuronal cultures and the mature brain.

entries.proposition: The metabolomics sampled cortex only and could not separate neuron-intrinsic from systemic or behavioural effects.
entries.snippet: Finally, a limitation of our metabolomic data is that we only analyzed brain samples.

entries.proposition: Direct rapamycin inhibition does not protect when mTOR is not hyperactive, per the cited work.
entries.snippet: However, direct mTOR inhibition by rapamycin is insufficient to protect from seizures when mTOR is not hyperactive (Hartman et al., 2012).
